doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

title: Bass and trombone, moving the root, and McCoy Tyner's altered chord
summary: Turré explains how moving the root changes harmonic color and tells how McCoy Tyner showed him the minor-major seventh scale for altered chords.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The fact that you played a melodic instrument plus you played the bass, I would think that that gave you an added perspective on how music worked, and you’re hearing the, providing the bass notes and hearing the chords on top of it. I’m not sure there’s a question here except that I think the bass is so important to all the music we play and improvisation also — being able to hear the low end.

Well you know in New Orleans traditional music the trombone is like a quasi-bass at times. And you know you touch on the bass and then you go up and do some other stuff, but it’s connected. And of course you know you don’t have a chord without a root, you know, but then you know as my ears have developed you can take a chord and move the root around. And the colors change but it’s still the same chord. You know I’ll tell you something I played with Dizzy, McCoy Tyner, Woody Shaw, Cedar, all the — we never, we never talk about modes, oh that’s a Mixolydian mode, oh that’s a Locrian mode. It’s a

B flat scale but you’re starting on an E or E flat or whatever. It’s just, that’s the color. That’s the tonality. By moving the root you change the color. But you know, for instance, I was asking McCoy Tyner what he played on the — mostly they call it the altered chord. Altered how? What does altered mean? It’s the raise 5, raise 9. That’s what they mean. Plus 5, plus 9. You know a lot of McCoy’s music has that in there. And you know I could approximate the sound but there was something I was missing. And I asked him, I said, “What do you play on that chord?” And he said, “Well it’s a minor major seventh.” Let’s say if you got a C 7 raise 9, raise 5. You play E flat minor major seventh scale. That’s all it is. It’s simple. You don’t have to trouble your brain thinking about a flat 9 or a plus 9. It’s a D flat minor major seventh scale. Once you become fluent with that, against that root, you hear it and you just play it. You don’t think about it.
